lessons.title: പള്ളിക്കൂടം (paḷḷikkūṭaṁ) — a school
lessons.gloss: a school — the building named for two older buildings, and the place the teacher and the student you already know are standing in

segments.text: Say a teacher. Say a student. You have had both of them for a long while, and never once had the building they are standing in.
പള്ളിക്കൂടം (paḷḷikkūṭaṁ) — a school.

It is a long word, and it is long because it is two words. The first, paḷḷi, is what Malayalam calls a mosque or a church. The second, kūṭaṁ, is a hall. The ordinary everyday word for a school is a compound of two buildings.

That is not a coincidence, and it is not a metaphor either. Teaching happened where the community already gathered — the hall beside the place of worship was where children were taught, long before anybody built a separate building for it. The word kept the arrangement after the arrangement changed.
Kerala has a second word too, borrowed straight from English and heard constantly. This one is the native compound, and it is the one that tells you something.

segments.instruction: the two words it is made of, and what each one means
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the two words it is made of, and what each one means]

segments.instruction: the teacher, the student, and the building
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the teacher, the student, and the building]

segments.text: A school? (പള്ളിക്കൂടം (paḷḷikkūṭaṁ).) What are the two words inside it? (paḷḷi, a place of worship, and kūṭaṁ, a hall.) Who is in it that you could already name? (അധ്യാപകൻ and വിദ്യാർത്ഥി.)

lessons.title: പാഠം (pāṭhaṁ) — a lesson
lessons.gloss: a lesson — and a word that tells you in advance what it will do when a case ending arrives

segments.text: Say a school. Then say what happens to -ം when a case ending is added to the word.
പാഠം (pāṭhaṁ) — a lesson, the kind a school gives you: a chapter of a book, a thing to be learned.
The Sanskrit it comes from means a recitation — a saying-aloud. The lesson was named for the saying, not for the page it is written on, which is worth knowing about a word you are about to say aloud.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: you already know what it will do

segments.text: പാഠം (pāṭhaṁ) ends in -ം, and that tells you something before you are taught it. When a case ending is added, the -ം gives way to -ത്ത-:
പാഠം (pāṭhaṁ) becomes പാഠത്തിൽ (pāṭhattil) — in the lesson.
That is the same rule, unchanged, that the state name and the book followed. You are not learning a new behaviour; you are meeting a new word that already belongs to a family you know.

segments.instruction: pāṭhaṁ, then pāṭhattil — and name what changed
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *pāṭhaṁ*, then *pāṭhattil* — and name what changed]

segments.instruction: what the Sanskrit behind it means
segments.source: [YOU SAY: what the Sanskrit behind it means]

segments.text: A lesson? (പാഠം (pāṭhaṁ).) What does its -ം become when a case ending is added? (-ത്ത- — പാഠത്തിൽ.) What did the Sanskrit word behind it mean? (A recitation.)

lessons.title: പരീക്ഷ (parīkṣa) — an exam
lessons.gloss: an exam — a Sanskrit word for looking closely at something, and one that does NOT end in the anusvara

segments.text: Say a lesson. Then say the apology you have had since early on — and listen for the ക്ഷ in the middle of it.
പരീക്ഷ (parīkṣa) — an exam.
You can already write the hard part. The ക്ഷ in the middle is the one that opens that apology. It is not a new shape; it is a shape you have been saying since the beginning, sitting in a new word.
The Sanskrit behind it is pari- (around) plus a root meaning to look. An examination is a looking all around something.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: this one does not end in -ം

segments.text: The word before this one ended in -ം and told you what it would do. This one ends in അ, and it does not join the same family:

Two words from the same chapter, in the same subject, behaving differently. That is worth noticing rather than smoothing over: what a Malayalam word does when something attaches to it is decided by how it ends, not by what it means.

segments.instruction: the apology, then the exam — and name the shape they share
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the apology, then the exam — and name the shape they share]

segments.instruction: pāṭhaṁ, then parīkṣa, and how each one ends
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *pāṭhaṁ*, then *parīkṣa*, and how each one ends]

segments.text: An exam? (പരീക്ഷ (parīkṣa).) Which earlier word shares its middle shape? (That apology, ക്ഷമിക്കണം.) Which of this chapter's two words ends in -ം? (പാഠം (pāṭhaṁ) — not പരീക്ഷ (parīkṣa).)

lessons.title: മാർക്ക് (mārkkŭ) — marks
lessons.gloss: marks — an English word that put on Malayalam clothes, and whose ending you have written many times

segments.text: Say an exam. Then count in tens — you will want the numbers in a moment.
മാർക്ക് (mārkkŭ) — marks, what an exam gives back to you.

Say it out loud and you will hear English. It is the English word mark, borrowed whole. Kerala's schools took the English examination system and the English word along with it, and this is the word people reach for.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: what the borrowing had to change

segments.text: The word is English, and the spelling is not. Two things happened to it on the way in, and you can see both:
the ർ before a doubled ക്ക — the shape you already write in ശർക്കര and ചേർക്കുക;
the half-u at the end, the faint vowel that closes so many Malayalam words and that English mark does not have at all.
A borrowed word does not stay foreign. It is made to end the way Malayalam words end, and then it behaves like one.

segments.instruction: mārkkŭ, and hear the English inside it
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *mārkkŭ*, and hear the English inside it]

segments.instruction: parīkṣa, then mārkkŭ — the exam, then what it gives back
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *parīkṣa*, then *mārkkŭ* — the exam, then what it gives back]

segments.instruction: a number in tens, then mārkkŭ
segments.source: [YOU SAY: a number in tens, then *mārkkŭ*]

segments.text: Marks? (മാർക്ക് (mārkkŭ).) Where does the word come from? (English — mark.) What two things did Malayalam do to its spelling? (The chillu ർ before the doubled ക്ക, and the half-u at the end.)

lessons.title: (school, lesson, exam, marks) (paḷḷikkūṭaṁ enna ōrmma) — from cold
lessons.gloss: cold retrieval of the four school words, and of the three different places they came from

segments.text: Close the lessons before this one. Say school, lesson, exam and marks.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: four words, three different origins

segments.text: One small corner of one subject, and the words in it came from three places:

utterances: പള്ളിക്കൂടം, paḷḷikkūṭaṁ, a compound of two buildings.

segments.text: That is what a school vocabulary looks like in Malayalam, and it is not untidy — it is a record. The building is named the old way, the scholarly words came with the scholarly tradition, and the examination system arrived with its own word attached.

You had the people before you had the place. The teacher and the student have been yours for a long while with nothing around them; now there is a building, a thing taught in it, a test of the thing, and a number at the end.

And the two Sanskrit words do not behave alike: പാഠം (pāṭhaṁ) ends in -ം and gives way to -ത്ത- when a case ending arrives; പരീക്ഷ (parīkṣa) ends in അ and does no such thing. Same subject, same origin, different endings — and the ending is what decides.

segments.instruction: which of the four is English, and which two are Sanskrit
segments.source: [YOU SAY: which of the four is English, and which two are Sanskrit]

segments.instruction: the teacher and the student, now inside the building
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the teacher and the student, now inside the building]

segments.text: School, exam, marks? (പള്ളിക്കൂടം (paḷḷikkūṭaṁ), പരീക്ഷ (parīkṣa), മാർക്ക് (mārkkŭ).) Which one is English? (മാർക്ക് (mārkkŭ).) Which word in the chapter changes when a case ending arrives, and to what? (പാഠം (pāṭhaṁ) becomes പാഠത്തിൽ.)
